newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Oil price jolts mirror Iraq tensions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil price jolts mirror Iraq tensions.

text.p: Oil markets betting on a new U.S. military assault against Iraq drove prices higher Thursday, ending a day fraught with tension and unease on what lies ahead for the world's preeminent oil producing region.

Values were boosted to a new five-year high close on the consistent barrage of headlines depicting a defiant Iraq, claiming to have again shot missiles at U.S. warplanes patroling no-fly zones in the southern portion of the country.
Iraq also warned U.S. ally Kuwait against basing American fighter jets on its soil, raising the possibility the conflict between the U.S. and Iraq may spread to other oil-rich nations.
Even as the market digested Iraqi claims, Washington announced "Stealth" advanced fighter jets were heading to the Persian Gulf, and vowed U.S. resolve to settle the conflict.

October spot oil futures contracts on the New York Mercantile Exchange ended Thursday 25 cents per barrel (bbl) higher at $25.00 bbl, after topping earlier at $25.30 bbl, near the five-year spot high set in April at $25.70.
"Clearly, it is a fear-driven market and I think the shorts are loath to sell it until we get definitive news," said Andrew Lebow, an oil trader for E.D. & F. Man International Inc in New York.
Lebow said the consensus for a new round of U.S. strikes against Saddam's military were extremely high.
"Everyone is anticipating a strike, its probably the most advertised military action ever. But the fear is usaully worse than the actual event," for the market, Lebow said.
Still, oil prices fluctuated wildly Thursday. Traders said profit-taking, and technical indicators, pressured many to take profits on the bullish run above the $25.00 bbl mark.
A Texas cash crude trader said the more bearish technical sector of the market, the one not reliant on news headlines for forecasting price direction, was reflected in the price retreats.
"All substantial technical indicators show this market ready for a $2-$3 barrel downturn," the trader said. "The technical people are all saying this market has a lot to give back," he added.
But even a substanitally overbought market has to take a back seat to the tensions in the world's most prolific oil patch, oil traders noted.
Iraq's military revitalization has also delayed implementation of the U.N. oil-for-food accord, which would have put some 700,000 barrels of additonal crude on the market in September.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali suspended the accord on September 1, saying the resumption of the humanitarian aid plan would resume only when conditions on the ground were safe for U.N. personnel meant to monitor the deal.
